questions.question: Which two Greek words combine to form the word 'philosophy'?

options.B: Philos and Sophia
options.C: Philos and Mythos

questions.explanation: The word philosophy comes from the Greek words 'Philos' (love) and 'Sophia' (the love of wisdom).

questions.question: What does the Greek word 'Philos' mean?

options.B: Truth
options.C: Love

questions.explanation: 'Philos' simply means 'love' in Greek.

questions.question: What does the Greek word 'Sophia' mean?

options.B: The love of wisdom
options.C: The pursuit of truth

questions.explanation: 'Sophia' means 'the love of wisdom,' giving philosophy its foundational meaning.

questions.question: From its Greek roots, philosophy can best be described as what kind of pursuit?

options.A: A spiritual search for divine truth
options.B: A rational search for the ideal life and how it should be lived practically
options.C: A scientific inquiry into the natural world
options.D: A political search for justice and governance

questions.explanation: From its Greek roots (Philos + Sophia), philosophy is understood as a rational search for the ideal life and how that ideal life has to be lived in practical terms.

questions.question: Which scholar viewed philosophy as a rational search for ultimate reality and the truth about the basic questions of life?

options.B: Jose Gasset
options.C: Fulmer

questions.explanation: Fulmer (2003) defined philosophy as the rational search for ultimate reality and truth about the basic questions of life in general and human life in particular.

questions.question: According to Fulmer (2003), which of the following is NOT an aspect of philosophical inquiry?

options.B: Day-to-day experiences of life
options.C: Mathematical proofs and theorems
options.D: The reasons and goals of living

questions.explanation: Fulmer's scope of philosophy covers human existence, daily experiences, reasons and goals of living, and the role of man and woman in the world — not mathematical theorems.

questions.question: Fulmer (2003) stated that philosophy involves an enquiry into all of the following EXCEPT:

options.A: The part played by men and women in the world
options.B: The existence of human beings
options.C: The economic systems of ancient civilizations
options.D: The reasons and goals of living

questions.explanation: Fulmer's definition covers human existence, daily experiences, reasons and goals of living, and humanity's role in the world. Economic systems are not part of this definition.

questions.question: What does the claim 'everyone is in one way or another a philosopher' most directly imply?

options.A: All people have formal training in philosophy
options.B: Philosophy is an activity in which all people are involved
options.C: Philosophy requires no intellectual effort
options.D: Only academics can truly define philosophy

questions.explanation: The text states that philosophy is an activity in which all are involved, which is why everyone can be considered a philosopher in some way.

questions.question: Why does philosophy have many definitions?

options.A: Because it is a new and undeveloped field
options.B: Because each philosopher defines it from their own point of view
options.C: Because ancient texts have been lost over time
options.D: Because it changes meaning across different languages

questions.explanation: There are as many definitions of philosophy as there are philosophers because everyone defines the subject matter from his or her own point of view.

questions.question: What was Aristotle's key point when he said one must philosophize whether they agree with philosophy or not?

options.A: That philosophy is only for the educated elite
options.B: That rejecting philosophy is itself a philosophical act
options.C: That philosophy should be taught in all schools
options.D: That philosophy and science are the same discipline

questions.explanation: Aristotle's quote implies that even arguing against philosophy requires philosophical reasoning — so in either case, one must philosophize.

questions.question: Which scholars cited Aristotle's famous quote about the inescapability of philosophizing?

options.B: Oyeshile and Ugwuanyi
options.C: Sophia and Philos

questions.explanation: Oyeshile & Ugwuanyi (2006) cited Aristotle's statement about the necessity of philosophizing.

questions.question: What year did Oyeshile and Ugwuanyi publish their work referencing Aristotle's quote on philosophy?
questions.explanation: Oyeshile & Ugwuanyi (2006) is the citation given in the text.

questions.question: Critics of philosophy who call it absurd or a waste of time are, ironically, doing what?

options.B: Engaging in philosophical reasoning themselves
options.C: Practicing science instead of philosophy

questions.explanation: Aristotle's logic shows that even criticizing philosophy as absurd requires reasoning and argument — which is itself philosophizing.

questions.question: Some critics describe philosophy as the use of high-sounding words ending in '-isms' and '-tions' that lead to what outcome?

options.B: Empty grammatical acrobatics
options.C: Political revolutions

questions.explanation: The text notes the criticism that philosophy involves high-sounding words ending in 'isms' and 'tions' that lead to empty grammatical acrobatics.

questions.question: What critical view is presented about some philosophers' use of complex intellectual language?

options.A: It effectively communicates truth to all audiences
options.B: It is the most rigorous form of academic writing
options.C: It is an art of cunningly convincing people through impressive-sounding but wasteful arguments
options.D: It proves that philosophy surpasses all other disciplines

questions.explanation: The text describes a critical view that some philosophers use complex language as an art of cunningly convincing people through words and arguments that ultimately end in a waste of time.

questions.question: Despite differing definitions of philosophy, what factor qualifies someone as a philosopher according to the text?

options.A: Having a university degree in the humanities
options.B: Giving reasons to justify a position or postulation
options.C: Memorizing the works of ancient Greek thinkers

questions.explanation: The text states that the reason one gives to justify any position or postulation is what makes someone a philosopher.

questions.question: What nationality was the philosopher Jose Gasset, mentioned in the text?

options.B: French
options.C: Spanish

questions.explanation: The text describes Jose Gasset as a Spanish philosopher.

questions.question: Which ancient Greek philosopher is quoted in the text regarding the unavoidability of philosophy?

options.B: Plato
options.C: Aristotle

questions.explanation: Aristotle is the Greek philosopher quoted as saying one must philosophize in either case — whether one agrees with philosophy or not.

questions.question: What year did Fulmer publish his definition of philosophy referenced in the text?
questions.explanation: The text cites Fulmer (2003) for the definition of philosophy as a rational search for ultimate reality and truth.

questions.question: Which of the following best captures the broad scope of philosophy as described by Fulmer?

options.A: It is limited to the study of language and grammar
options.B: It covers ultimate reality, human existence, daily life, goals of living, and humanity's role in the world
options.C: It focuses exclusively on political and economic systems
options.D: It is concerned only with metaphysical and religious questions

questions.explanation: Fulmer's definition encompasses the search for ultimate reality, truth about life in general and human life specifically, human existence, day-to-day experiences, reasons and goals of living, and the role of men and women in the world.

questions.question: What does the word 'PHILOSOPHY' literally mean?

options.B: Pursuit of wisdom
options.C: Search for truth

questions.explanation: The word PHILOSOPHY means pursuit of wisdom, where wisdom refers to good judgments and understanding of what is true, right, and enduring.

questions.question: What does 'wisdom' specifically refer to in the context of philosophy?

options.A: The accumulation of factual knowledge over time
options.B: The ability to memorize philosophical texts
options.C: Good judgments and understanding of what is true, right, and timeless
options.D: The capacity to debate and argue effectively

questions.explanation: Wisdom is defined as good judgments and understanding of what is true, what is right, and what can stand the test of time.

questions.question: What was cited as the original name for philosophy?

options.B: Wisdom
options.C: Truth

questions.explanation: A philosopher noted that the original name for philosophy was 'the truth,' leading to philosophy being defined as an attempt to place us in contact with naked reality itself.

questions.question: How was philosophy defined in relation to reality?

options.A: A systematic method for constructing reality
options.B: An attempt to place us in contact with naked reality itself
options.C: A discipline that helps us escape from objective reality
options.D: A framework for categorizing aspects of reality

questions.explanation: Philosophy was defined as an attempt to place us in contact with naked reality itself — engaging directly with reality as it is, without pretense.

questions.question: What does the study of philosophy guarantee for individuals?

options.B: They will become better educators
options.C: They will find answers to life's questions
options.D: It does not guarantee any of the above

questions.explanation: The study of philosophy does not guarantee that individuals will be better thinkers or better educators. It only provides a valuable base to help us think more clearly.

questions.question: What does philosophy provide, despite not guaranteeing improved thinking or teaching?

options.A: A complete framework of moral rules
options.B: Definitive answers to intellectual questions
options.C: A valuable base to help us think more clearly
options.D: A structured pathway to academic success

questions.explanation: Although philosophy does not guarantee better thinking or teaching, it provides a valuable base to help us think more clearly.

questions.question: What is the primary role of philosophy in relation to answers and inquiry?

options.A: It provides definitive answers to all philosophical questions
options.B: It offers an avenue for serious inquiry into ideas and traditions, not definitive answers
options.C: It discourages inquiry by establishing fixed doctrines
options.D: It focuses only on answering practical life questions

questions.explanation: Philosophy does not imply that it provides answers. Rather, it offers an avenue for serious inquiry into ideas and traditions.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes philosophers as observers?

options.B: Acute observers of human conditions who articulate their observations instructively
options.C: Critics focused exclusively on social and political systems
options.D: Casual commentators on everyday human behavior

questions.explanation: Philosophers have been described as acute observers of human conditions who have articulated their observations in ways that are instructive.

questions.question: How do educators benefit from philosophy?

options.A: Philosophy provides educators with ready-made lesson plans
options.B: Philosophy aids educators with a careful, systematic approach to ideas and develops new insights into educational problems
options.C: Philosophy replaces the need for formal pedagogical training
options.D: Philosophy helps educators avoid controversial subjects

questions.explanation: Educators are aided by the careful and systematic approach to ideas fostered by philosophers, and they also gain inspiration from philosophy to develop new insights into educational problems.

questions.question: How is 'Philosophy of Education' best defined?

options.A: The history of educational institutions from ancient times
options.B: The branch of philosophy focused solely on the logic of learning
options.C: The application of philosophical ideas to solve problems in education and the larger society
options.D: A discipline that studies how philosophers were educated

questions.explanation: Philosophy of education is defined as the application of philosophical ideas to solve problems in education and the larger society.

questions.question: According to Jaspers (1972), what type of action is philosophy?

options.B: An inner action through which a thinker comes to authentic awareness of themselves and reality
options.C: A collective intellectual exercise performed in academic institutions
options.D: A purely logical process of deductive reasoning

questions.explanation: Jaspers views philosophy as a process of thinking — an inner action — by which the thinker arrives at an authentic awareness of themselves and reality.

questions.question: How does Jaspers describe the process by which a philosopher achieves awareness?

options.A: By accepting and working within existing objective frameworks
options.B: By memorizing the works of established philosophers
options.C: By pressing beyond or transcending everything objective
options.D: By conducting empirical research and experiments

questions.explanation: According to Jaspers, the thinker comes to authentic awareness of themselves and reality by pressing beyond or transcending everything objective.

questions.question: How does Jaspers differentiate philosophy from disciplines like psychology or anthropology?

options.A: Philosophy is more scientifically rigorous than those disciplines
options.B: Philosophy deals exclusively with ancient knowledge
options.C: Unlike those disciplines, philosophy is not a settled piece of knowledge — it is evolving and expanding
options.D: Philosophy focuses only on human behavior, unlike those disciplines

questions.explanation: Jaspers argues that philosophy, unlike psychology or anthropology, is not a settled piece of knowledge. It is continuously evolving and expanding.

questions.question: What is Heidegger's view on the relationship between philosophy and values?

options.A: Philosophy reinforces and protects societal values
options.B: Philosophy is neutral and does not affect values
options.C: Philosophy threatens and questions every value held by people
options.D: Philosophy creates new values to replace outdated ones

questions.explanation: Heidegger views philosophy as the discipline that keeps questioning everything, thereby threatening every value held by people.

questions.question: How does Heidegger define philosophy?

options.A: The systematic collection and analysis of human knowledge
options.B: Thinking that breaks paths and hierarchies of knowledge, kindles all inquiries, and threatens human and societal values
options.C: An inner journey toward self-discovery through meditation
options.D: The pursuit of consensus among thinkers about ultimate reality

questions.explanation: Heidegger defines philosophy as thinking that breaks the paths and hierarchies of knowledge in which a person fulfills himself historically and culturally — knowledge that kindles and necessitates all inquiries and threatens all human and societal values.

questions.question: In Heidegger's view, how does a person fulfill themselves through philosophy?

options.B: Academically and professionally
options.C: Historically and culturally

questions.explanation: According to Heidegger, a person fulfills himself historically and culturally through the kind of knowledge that philosophy represents.

questions.question: What characterizes the philosophical thinkers whose postulations are considered profound and enduring?

options.A: They belong to a single dominant civilization
options.B: They are all from European intellectual traditions
options.C: They are found in different parts of the world and different professions of life
options.D: They exclusively focus on political and economic thought

questions.explanation: Great philosophical minds are found in different parts of the world and in different professions of life — no single nation or civilization holds a monopoly on such thinkers.

questions.question: Which of the following is true about the global distribution of great philosophical minds?

options.A: Western nations have produced the majority of great philosophers
options.B: No nation or part of the world has a monopoly on great philosophical minds
options.C: Philosophy is predominantly an Eastern intellectual tradition
options.D: Great philosophical thought is concentrated in academic institutions

questions.explanation: No nation or part of the world has a monopoly on great philosophical minds. They are found globally and across different professions.

questions.question: Which of the following thinkers is NOT listed among the great philosophical names mentioned?

options.B: Aristotle
options.C: Confucius

questions.explanation: The great names listed are Socrates, Plato, Archimedes, Buddha, and Confucius. Aristotle is not mentioned in this passage.

questions.question: What do upcoming thinkers seek from established great philosophical minds?

options.B: Philosophical skills
options.C: Political guidance

questions.explanation: Upcoming thinkers go to established great philosophical minds specifically to acquire 'philosophical skills.'

questions.question: Where did philosophy originate, according to the consensus of most philosophers?

options.A: The Nile Delta of ancient Egypt
options.B: The Indian subcontinent
options.C: Ancient Greek civilization

questions.explanation: Most philosophers — including Bertrand Russell, Copestone, Burnet, Armstrong, and Hammocks — agree that philosophy originated from ancient Greek civilization.

questions.question: Approximately when did philosophy originate?

options.B: Around 590 B.C.
options.C: Around 690 B.C.

questions.explanation: Philosophy is said to have originated around 690 B.C. when men in the Island of Ionia near Greece began to probe into the world of ultimate reality.

questions.question: Where specifically did the early probing into ultimate reality take place that marked the beginning of philosophy?

options.A: The Island of Sicily near Italy
options.B: The Island of Ionia near Greece
options.C: The Peninsula of Attica in mainland Greece
options.D: The Island of Cyprus in the Mediterranean

questions.explanation: The early philosophical inquiry that gave birth to philosophy began with men in the Island of Ionia near Greece.

questions.question: What were the early philosophers in Ionia probing into?

options.A: The laws of nature and physical phenomena
options.B: Political systems and governance structures
options.C: The world of ultimate reality

questions.explanation: The men in the Island of Ionia began to probe into the world of ultimate reality, which marked the beginning of philosophy.

questions.question: Which of the following philosophers is among those credited with establishing that philosophy originated in ancient Greece?

options.B: Bertrand Russell
options.C: John Dewey

questions.explanation: Bertrand Russell is among the philosophers (along with Copestone, Burnet, Armstrong, and Hammocks) who agree that philosophy originated from ancient Greek civilization around 690 B.C.

questions.question: Which view of philosophy emphasizes its role as a continuously evolving discipline rather than a fixed body of knowledge?

options.B: The Greek origin view
options.C: Jaspers' view

questions.explanation: Jaspers specifically emphasized that philosophy is not a settled piece of knowledge like psychology or anthropology — it is evolving and keeps expanding.

questions.question: Which philosopher is most associated with the view that philosophy disrupts established knowledge hierarchies?

options.B: Martin Heidegger
options.C: Bertrand Russell

questions.explanation: Martin Heidegger specifically defined philosophy as thinking that breaks the paths and hierarchies of knowledge, challenging established intellectual and societal structures.

questions.question: What distinguishes the way Jaspers (1972) approaches philosophy from a purely academic standpoint?

options.A: Jaspers sees philosophy as a social and communal activity
options.B: Jaspers views philosophy as an inner, personal process of achieving authentic self-awareness
options.C: Jaspers believes philosophy should focus only on empirical evidence
options.D: Jaspers argues that philosophy must be grounded in political theory

questions.explanation: Jaspers' distinctive approach is that philosophy is an inner action — a deeply personal process through which the thinker arrives at authentic awareness of themselves and reality, going beyond purely academic or objective frameworks.

questions.question: A student argues that once enough philosophical texts are studied, philosophy becomes a complete and settled discipline. Which thinker's view most directly contradicts this?

options.B: Bertrand Russell
options.C: Karl Jaspers

questions.explanation: Jaspers explicitly states that philosophy is not a settled piece of knowledge like psychology or anthropology. It is evolving and keeps expanding — directly contradicting the idea that it can ever be fully settled.

questions.question: A teacher uses philosophical ideas to redesign the school curriculum to better address social inequality. This best exemplifies which concept?

options.B: Philosophy of education
options.C: Philosophical skepticism

questions.explanation: Using philosophical ideas to solve educational and societal problems — such as redesigning a curriculum to address inequality — is the definition of philosophy of education.

questions.question: Which philosopher is credited with predicting a solar eclipse and is recognized as a great astronomer and geographer?

options.B: Anaximander
options.C: Thales of Miletus

questions.explanation: Thales of Miletus, a 6th century B.C. philosopher, was recognized as a great astronomer and geographer and is remembered for his prediction of a solar eclipse.

questions.question: What did Thales of Miletus base his cosmological insights on?

options.B: What he regarded as the essence of all matter
options.C: The relationship between faith and reason

questions.explanation: Thales based his cosmological insights on what he regarded as the essence of all matter.

questions.question: Which historical period does the ancient pre-Socratic era span?

questions.question: What were the pre-Socratic philosophers primarily concerned with?

options.B: Reconciling science with religion
options.C: Discovering the basic nature of reality

questions.explanation: The philosophers of the pre-Socratic epoch, popularly known as cosmologists, were more interested in discovering the basic nature of reality.

questions.question: What popular term was used to describe the pre-Socratic philosophers?

options.B: Cosmologists
options.C: Empiricists

questions.explanation: The philosophers of the pre-Socratic epoch were popularly known as cosmologists.

questions.question: Which of the following philosophers belonged to the pre-Socratic period?

options.B: Aristotle
options.C: Zeno

questions.question: Which philosopher is described as a pupil of Socrates?

options.B: Plato
options.C: Anaximander

questions.question: What label was given to Socrates, Plato, and Aristotle due to their immense influence?

options.A: Philosophers of the Age of Enlightenment
options.B: Founders of the Renaissance
options.C: Philosophers of the Golden Age of Greece

questions.explanation: Socrates, Plato, and Aristotle were known as the philosophers of the Golden Age of Greece.

questions.question: What was Socrates' key argument about the purpose of human philosophical inquiry?

options.A: Man should seek to understand the cosmos
options.B: Man should pursue political power through wisdom
options.C: Man should prioritize the quest for self-knowledge over searching for ultimate reality
options.D: Man should reconcile faith and reason

questions.explanation: Socrates argued that instead of immersing himself in the search for ultimate reality, man should be busy with the quest for self-knowledge.

questions.question: Which institution dominated philosophical thought during the Medieval Period?

options.B: The Church
options.C: Royal academies

questions.explanation: Philosophy during the Medieval Period (1100–1400 A.D.) was dominated by the church father, and the prevailing situations helped consolidate the Christian faith.

questions.question: What time period corresponds to the Medieval Period in philosophy?
questions.explanation: The Middle Ages or Medieval Period in philosophy spans from 1100 A.D. to 1400 A.D.

questions.question: What was the central theme of philosophical discourse during the Medieval Period?

options.A: The nature of matter and the cosmos
options.B: The relationship between faith and reason
options.C: The rights of individuals in society

questions.explanation: Most of the philosophical discourse of the Medieval Period had to do with the relationship between faith and reason, or broadly between philosophy and theology.

questions.question: Which of the following was a Medieval philosopher?

options.B: Rene Descartes
options.C: St. Thomas Aquinas

questions.question: Al-farabi is categorized among which group of thinkers in the history of philosophy?

options.C: Arabic philosophers of the Medieval Period

questions.question: What major intellectual challenge characterized the Renaissance of Philosophy (1450–1600)?

options.B: Reconciling science with philosophy
options.C: Defending the church against secular thought

questions.explanation: During the Renaissance of Philosophy, scientific discoveries were springing up and there was a need to reconcile science with philosophy.

questions.question: Who is regarded as the pioneer of modern philosophical thought?

options.B: Rene Descartes
options.C: Francis Bacon

questions.explanation: Francis Bacon, an outstanding philosopher of the Renaissance era, is known as the pioneer of modern philosophical thought.

questions.question: What famous maxim is attributed to Francis Bacon?

options.B: "Knowledge is power"
options.C: "The unexamined life is not worth living"
options.D: "Man is the measure of all things"

questions.explanation: Francis Bacon is credited with the maxim "knowledge is power."

questions.question: How did Francis Bacon describe himself?

options.B: The pioneer of empiricism
options.C: The trumpeter of the new science

questions.explanation: Francis Bacon referred to himself as "the trumpeter of the new science."

questions.question: Rene Descartes is popularly known by which title?

options.B: The father of modernism
options.C: The father of rationalism

questions.explanation: Rene Descartes, the great French philosopher, is popularly called the father of modernism.

questions.question: What is the philosophical significance of Descartes' statement "I think therefore I am"?

options.A: It established the supremacy of religious faith
options.B: It served as the foundation of his political theory
options.C: It was an enduring result of his search for truth and certainty
options.D: It summarized his theory of cosmology

questions.explanation: Descartes' thesis "I think therefore I am" served as an enduring result of his search for truth and certainty.

questions.question: Thomas Hobbes is best known for writing which major philosophical work?

options.B: Essay Concerning Human Understanding
options.C: The Leviathan

questions.explanation: Thomas Hobbes was a philosopher of the rationalistic and empiricist school of thought who wrote the Leviathan.

questions.question: Which philosopher wrote the "Essay Concerning Human Understanding"?

options.B: David Hume
options.C: Thomas Hobbes

questions.explanation: John Locke wrote the Essay Concerning Human Understanding and belongs to the rationalistic and empiricist school of thought.

questions.question: Which schools of thought did Thomas Hobbes, John Locke, George Berkeley, and David Hume belong to?

options.B: Rationalistic and empiricist schools
options.C: Scholasticism and theology

questions.explanation: These philosophers all belonged to the rationalistic and empiricist schools of thought.

questions.question: What time period does late modern philosophy cover?
questions.explanation: Late modern philosophies cover the period 1700–1900 A.D.

questions.question: What was Immanuel Kant's major contribution to late modern philosophy?

options.A: He founded the empiricist school of thought
options.B: He reconciled rationalism and empiricism and wrote Critique of Pure Reason
options.C: He established the dominance of theology in philosophy
options.D: He developed the cosmological theory of matter

questions.explanation: Immanuel Kant's work in the late modern period involved Recording Rationalism and Empiricism, and he wrote Critique of Pure Reason to support his arguments.

questions.question: Which of the following is the correct chronological order of philosophical periods?

options.B: Pre-Socratic → Classical Socratic → Medieval → Renaissance → Early Modern → Late Modern
options.C: Classical Socratic → Pre-Socratic → Medieval → Late Modern → Renaissance
options.D: Renaissance → Medieval → Pre-Socratic → Classical Socratic → Late Modern

questions.explanation: The correct order is Pre-Socratic (600 B.C.–103 A.D.) → Classical Socratic/Platonic → Medieval (1100–1400) → Renaissance (1450–1600) → Early Modern (16th–17th century) → Late Modern (1700–1900).

questions.question: Which philosophical era immediately preceded the Renaissance of Philosophy?

options.B: Classical Socratic/Platonic era
options.C: Medieval period

questions.explanation: The Medieval Period (1100–1400 A.D.) preceded the Renaissance of Philosophy (1450–1600).

questions.question: How does Socrates' philosophical focus differ from that of the pre-Socratic cosmologists?

options.A: Socrates focused on cosmology while pre-Socratics focused on ethics
options.B: Socrates focused on self-knowledge while pre-Socratics focused on the basic nature of reality
options.C: Socrates focused on theology while pre-Socratics focused on science
options.D: Socrates focused on political theory while pre-Socratics focused on mathematics

questions.explanation: Pre-Socratics were interested in the basic nature of reality (cosmology), while Socrates argued that man should focus on the quest for self-knowledge.

questions.question: Which of the following philosophers is NOT associated with the pre-Socratic period?

options.C: Zenophanes

questions.explanation: St. Bonaventure belongs to the Medieval Period, not the pre-Socratic era.

questions.question: What distinguishes the early 16th and 17th century philosophical period from the Renaissance?

options.A: The earlier period focused on science while the later focused on self-knowledge
options.B: The earlier period features key individual thinkers like Descartes rather than the broader science-philosophy reconciliation of the Renaissance
options.C: The earlier period was dominated by the church while the later was secular
options.D: There is no distinction; they are the same period

questions.question: Which German philosopher is credited with taking idealism to greater heights and is known as the originator of absolute idealism?

options.B: Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel
options.C: Friedrich Nietzsche

questions.explanation: Hegel came after Kant and took idealism to greater heights. He is specifically identified as the originator of absolute idealism.

questions.question: Karl Marx is best described as a disciple of which philosopher?

options.B: John Stuart Mill
options.C: Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel

questions.explanation: Karl Marx was a popular disciple of Hegel. He adapted Hegel's philosophical framework for his own work.

questions.question: Karl Marx adapted Hegel's philosophical triad into which domain?

options.B: Religious philosophy
options.C: Economic terms

questions.explanation: Marx translated the Hegelian triad of thesis, antithesis, and synthesis into economic terms and viewed reality from a materialistic point of view.

questions.question: What is the philosophical triad that Karl Marx translated into economic terms?

options.B: Thesis, Antithesis, Synthesis
options.C: Idea, Matter, Spirit

questions.explanation: The Hegelian triad consists of thesis, antithesis, and synthesis. Marx adapted this dialectical structure into his materialistic economic analysis.

questions.question: From which philosophical standpoint did Karl Marx view reality?

options.B: Rationalistic point of view
options.C: Empiricist point of view

questions.explanation: Marx looked at reality from the materialistic point of view, contrasting with Hegel's idealism despite using the same dialectical framework.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT listed as a late modern philosopher?

options.B: Jeremy Bentham
options.C: Rudolf Carnap

questions.explanation: Rudolf Carnap is associated with the contemporary period (logical positivism/empiricism), not the late modern period. Mill, Bentham, Nietzsche, Kierkegaard, and Comte are listed as late modern philosophers.

questions.question: Which of the following philosophers is included among the late modern period thinkers?

options.B: Martin Heidegger
options.C: August Comte

questions.explanation: August Comte is listed among the late modern philosophers. Husserl, Heidegger, and Ayer belong to the contemporary period.

questions.question: The contemporary period of philosophy is said to have begun at what point in history?

options.B: The dawn of the 20th century
options.C: The middle of the 20th century

questions.explanation: The contemporary period started at the dawn of the 20th century, marking a shift in dominant philosophical schools of thought.

questions.question: Which school of thought chiefly dominated the contemporary period of philosophy?

options.B: Absolute idealism
options.C: Epistemological school of thought

questions.explanation: The contemporary period was chiefly dominated by the epistemological school of thought, which encompasses logical positivism, analytical philosophy, and logical empiricism.

questions.question: Logical positivism and analytical philosophy are both associated with which broader philosophical movement?

options.B: Epistemological school of thought
options.C: Metaphysical idealism

questions.explanation: Logical positivism, analytical philosophy, and logical empiricism are all part of the epistemological school of thought that dominated the contemporary period.

questions.question: Who are the two philosophers credited with propagating logical empiricism in the contemporary period?

options.B: Edmund Husserl and Martin Heidegger
options.C: Rudolf Carnap and A.J. Ayer
options.D: Jean Paul Sartre and Soren Kierkegaard

questions.explanation: Rudolf Carnap and A.J. Ayer are credited with propagating logical empiricism during the contemporary period.

questions.question: American Pragmatism in the contemporary period was propagated by which pair of philosophers?

options.B: Edmund Husserl and Martin Heidegger

questions.explanation: Pantheists say God and the universe are identical — all are God and God is all. This view equates the divine with everything that exists.

questions.question: Which theological view sees God as the maker of nature and moral law but maintains that God is no longer interested in mankind and the universe?

options.B: Pantheism
options.C: Polytheism

questions.explanation: Deists see God as the maker of nature and moral law but assert that God exists apart from and is no longer interested in mankind and the universe — often called the 'clockmaker' view of God.

questions.question: What distinguishes Theists (Monotheists) from other theological positions?

options.A: They believe God created the universe but has since abandoned it
options.B: They believe in a personal Creator God and insist on only one God
options.C: They believe God and the universe are the same substance
options.D: They deny the existence of any supernatural beings

questions.explanation: Theists (Monotheists) believe in a personal Creator God and insist on only one God, distinguishing them from pantheists, deists, and polytheists.

questions.question: How does Polytheism differ from Monotheism?

options.A: Polytheists deny the existence of a greater God
options.B: Polytheists believe in more than one God, including lesser gods beneath a greater God
options.C: Polytheists believe God and the universe are one
options.D: Polytheists hold that God has no interest in human affairs

questions.explanation: Polytheists believe in more than one God — lesser gods before the greater God — in contrast to Monotheists who insist on only one God.

questions.question: Which beings, besides God, are mentioned as subjects of theological debate regarding their existence and relationship to God?

options.B: Angels, Satan, and the Holy Spirit
options.C: Ancestors, spirits, and demigods

questions.explanation: The text specifically asks whether there are such beings as angels, Satan, and the Holy Spirit, and what their relationship to God is — identifying these as ongoing theological questions.

questions.question: What is the Anthropological Aspect of metaphysics primarily the study of?

options.A: The nature of God and divine beings
options.B: The origin and structure of the universe
options.C: Man — with man as both the subject and object of inquiry
options.D: The nature of existence and what it means to be

questions.explanation: Anthropology (the Anthropological Aspect) is the study of man, where man is both the subject and the object of inquiry — when man philosophizes about man, he is speaking about himself.

questions.question: Which of the following is a central question raised by the Anthropological Aspect of metaphysics?

options.B: What is the relationship between mind and body?
options.C: Is there more than one God?
options.D: What is the nature of existence itself?

questions.explanation: The Anthropological Aspect asks: what is the relationship between mind and body? Is the mind more fundamental than the body, or vice versa? These are its central questions.

questions.question: When a philosopher asks whether the mind is more fundamental than the body, or whether the body depends on the mind, this falls under which aspect of metaphysics?

options.B: Ontological Aspect
options.C: Theological Aspect

questions.explanation: Questions about the interaction between mind and body, and which is more fundamental, are raised under the Anthropological Aspect of metaphysics.

questions.question: What does the Anthropological Aspect say about man's moral status, according to the Christian view?

options.A: Man is an accidental product of natural forces
options.B: Man's moral status is unknowable
options.C: Man is created in the image of God
options.D: Man's morality is determined by society alone

questions.explanation: While answers to anthropological questions are based on individual metaphysical beliefs, the text states that as Christians, man is created in the image of God.

questions.question: What does the Ontological Aspect of metaphysics study?

options.A: The existence and nature of God
options.B: The origin of the universe
options.C: The nature of existence — what it means for anything to be
options.D: The relationship between the human mind and body

questions.explanation: Ontology is the study of the nature of existence or what it means for anything to be. It is the most fundamental philosophical inquiry into what 'being' itself is.

questions.question: An ontological question would be:

options.A: How did the cosmos come into existence?
options.B: Is basic reality found in matter or something else?
options.C: What is man's moral responsibility?
options.D: Does God intervene in human history?

questions.explanation: The text specifically identifies 'Is basic reality found in matter or...' as an ontological question — it concerns the fundamental nature of what exists.

questions.question: The fact that a chemist, a physicist, and a poet each give a different description of the same floor best illustrates which philosophical point?

options.A: Science is superior to art in explaining reality
options.B: Questions about reality are more complex than they first appear
options.C: Only experts can understand the true nature of objects
options.D: Physical objects have no single true description

questions.explanation: The example of a floor being described differently by different people (as hydrocarbon, etc.) is used to show that the question of reality is not simple — if even a common floor is confusing, consider the larger problems of ultimate reality.

questions.question: A person's metaphysical beliefs are described in the text as coloring their:

options.B: Political and economic decisions
options.C: Comprehensive understanding of reality

questions.explanation: The text states that beliefs of people color their comprehensive understanding of reality — metaphysical beliefs shape how a person sees everything.

questions.question: Which of the following best captures the relationship between the Theological and Cosmological aspects of metaphysics?

options.A: They are completely unrelated areas of inquiry
options.B: Cosmology studies the universe's origins while theology examines God; both address ultimate questions about existence
options.C: Theology is a subset of cosmology
options.D: Cosmology replaces theology in modern philosophy

questions.explanation: Cosmology deals with the universe's origin and development while theology deals with God's existence and nature. Both are major aspects of metaphysics addressing ultimate questions about reality from different angles.

questions.question: Which of the following correctly pairs a metaphysical aspect with its core question?

options.A: Cosmology — What is man's moral status?
options.B: Ontology — How did the universe originate?
options.C: Anthropology — What is the relationship between mind and body?
options.D: Theology — What is the nature of existence itself?

questions.explanation: The Anthropological Aspect specifically raises the question of the relationship between mind and body. Cosmology covers universe origins, Ontology covers the nature of existence, and Theology covers God.

questions.question: A philosopher who believes that the body depends entirely on the mind would be engaging in which type of metaphysical inquiry?

options.B: Theological
options.C: Anthropological

questions.explanation: The question of whether the body depends on the mind (or vice versa) is explicitly raised within the Anthropological Aspect of metaphysics.

questions.question: Which theological position acknowledges God as creator but places God entirely outside and indifferent to the created world?

options.B: Pantheism
options.C: Polytheism

questions.explanation: Deists assert that God exists apart from and is no longer interested in mankind and the universe — God made the world but has since remained detached from it.

questions.question: What makes the philosophical investigation of a simple floor relevant to broader metaphysical questions?

options.A: It proves that physical objects are not real
options.B: It shows that even ordinary objects have complex and contested descriptions of reality, hinting at the depth of metaphysical inquiry
options.C: It demonstrates that chemistry is the basis of all knowledge
options.D: It reveals that science can answer all philosophical questions

questions.explanation: The floor example is used as a gateway: if something as ordinary as a floor prompts multiple valid descriptions of its reality (physical, chemical, aesthetic), then larger questions about ultimate reality are far more complex.

questions.question: When man philosophizes about man, the unique challenge is that:

options.A: Man lacks the intelligence to study himself
options.B: Man is both the subject studying and the object being studied
options.C: Man's physical body prevents philosophical thought
options.D: Man must rely entirely on divine revelation to understand himself

questions.explanation: The Anthropological Aspect notes that man is both the subject and the object of inquiry — this self-referential nature makes anthropological philosophy uniquely complex.

questions.question: Which of the following is a metaphysical question about the nature of ultimate reality?

options.A: How should a government be structured?
options.B: Is reality found in physical energy or in spirit?
options.C: What economic system best reduces poverty?
options.D: How should children be disciplined in schools?

questions.explanation: Metaphysical questions concern the nature of ultimate reality, such as whether it resides in physical/sensory energy or in spirit/spiritual energy.

questions.question: Which question best reflects a metaphysical inquiry about the stability of reality?

options.A: Is man born into a rich or poor family?
options.B: Is reality fixed and stable or is change its central feature?
options.C: Should education be publicly or privately funded?
options.D: Is man capable of scientific reasoning?

questions.explanation: Whether reality is fixed/stable or defined by change is a core metaphysical question about the nature of existence.

questions.question: When asking whether reality is 'friendly, unfriendly, or noble in regard to Man,' what domain of inquiry does this fall under?

options.B: Epistemology
options.C: Metaphysics

questions.explanation: The question of how reality relates to mankind — whether it is friendly, hostile, or neutral — is a metaphysical question about the nature of ultimate reality.

questions.question: The question of whether man possesses free will or whether his thoughts and actions are shaped by environment and inheritance is fundamentally a question about:

options.B: Human freedom and determinism
options.C: Social contract theory

questions.explanation: The debate over free will versus environmental/hereditary determinism is a classic metaphysical and philosophical question about human nature.

questions.question: What is the relationship between metaphysical positions and human social practices?

options.A: Metaphysical beliefs have no influence on social practices
options.B: Social practices shape metaphysical beliefs, never the reverse
options.C: Differing metaphysical positions are reflected in political, social, religious, and educational practices
options.D: Metaphysical beliefs only affect religious practices

questions.explanation: People adopt different positions on metaphysical questions, and these positions manifest in their political, social, religious, and educational practices and designs.

questions.question: In the Christian worldview, what serves as the self-revelation of the Creator-God?

options.B: Human reason and conscience
options.C: The Bible, through Jesus Christ

questions.explanation: Christians accept the Bible as the self-revelation of the Creator-God through Jesus Christ, which provides the metaphysical framework for Christian education.

questions.question: What role does biblical revelation play in Christian education according to the Christian worldview?

options.A: It provides only moral guidelines, not metaphysical ones
options.B: It enables further observations about reality and provides the metaphysical framework for education
options.C: It replaces all other forms of knowledge
options.D: It is one of many equally valid frameworks for education

questions.explanation: Biblical revelation allows Christians to make further observations about the nature of reality and provides the metaphysical framework within which Christian education takes place.

questions.question: Which of the following is listed as the FIRST pillar of the Biblical worldview?

options.A: The creation of man in God's image
options.B: The fall of man through Lucifer
options.C: The existence of the living Creator-God
options.D: The return of Christ at the end of history

questions.explanation: The first and foundational pillar of the Biblical worldview is the existence of the living Creator-God.

questions.question: According to the Biblical worldview, how is the created world originally described?

options.A: Flawed and in need of correction from the beginning
options.B: Morally neutral
options.C: Perfect, created by God

questions.explanation: One of the pillars of the Biblical worldview is the creation of a perfect world and universe by God.

questions.question: The Biblical pillar stating that man was made in the image of God is known by what Latin term?

options.B: Imago Dei
options.C: Homo Faber

questions.explanation: Man's creation in the image of God is classically referred to as Imago Dei in theological and philosophical traditions.

questions.question: What did Lucifer's act of 'forgetting his creatureliness' represent in the Biblical worldview?

options.B: The origin of sin — attempting to take God's place
options.C: The first human moral failure

questions.explanation: The 'invention' of sin is attributed to Lucifer, who forgot his own creatureliness and sought to place himself in the position of God.

questions.question: According to the Biblical worldview, how did sin enter the earth?

options.B: Through a collective human rebellion
options.C: Through the spread of sin by Lucifer, leading to the fall of man

questions.explanation: The Biblical worldview holds that sin spread to the earth through Lucifer, and the fall of man resulted in a partial loss of God's image.

questions.question: What was the consequence of the fall of man according to the Biblical worldview?

options.B: Total loss of God's image
options.C: Partial loss of God's image

questions.explanation: The fall of man resulted in a partial — not total — loss of God's image, according to the Biblical worldview.

questions.question: What does the Biblical worldview say about man's ability to restore God's image in himself without outside help?

options.A: Man can restore it through education and moral effort
options.B: Man can partially restore it through prayer alone
options.C: Man is unable, without divine aid, to change his nature or overcome inherent sinfulness
options.D: Man naturally regains God's image over time

questions.explanation: A key Biblical pillar is the inability of man, without divine aid, to change his own nature, overcome his inherent sinfulness, or restore the lost image of God.

questions.question: Which Biblical pillar addresses God taking the initiative in human history to address the problem of sin?

options.A: The creation of a perfect world
options.B: Man's creation in God's image
options.C: The initiative of God for the incarnation, life, death, and resurrection of Jesus Christ
options.D: The activity of the Holy Spirit in calling out the Church

questions.explanation: God's initiative in the incarnation, life, death, and resurrection of Jesus Christ is identified as a foundational Biblical pillar responding to human sinfulness.

questions.question: What is the described role of the Holy Spirit in the Biblical worldview?

options.A: To judge mankind at the end of time
options.B: To restore God's image in fallen man and call out the community of believers (the Church)
options.C: To inspire the writing of scripture only

questions.explanation: The activity of the Holy Spirit is described as the plan of restoring God's image in fallen man and His work in calling out the community of believers — the Church.

questions.question: What does the Biblical worldview identify as the ultimate future event at the end of earthly history?

options.B: The return of Christ
options.C: A global human moral reformation

questions.explanation: One of the pillars of the Biblical worldview is the return of Christ at the end of earthly history.

questions.question: What is the final state described in the Biblical worldview for the earth and its faithful inhabitants?

options.B: Eternal separation from the physical world
options.C: Restoration to an Edenic condition

questions.explanation: The final pillar of the Biblical worldview is the eventual restoration of the earth and its faithful inhabitants to an Edenic (Eden-like) condition.

questions.question: How many foundational pillars of the Biblical worldview are outlined in the text?
questions.explanation: The text lists 10 pillars of the Biblical worldview, labeled a through j.

questions.question: Why is metaphysics considered central to any concept of education?

options.A: Because it determines how teachers are paid
options.B: Because educational programs must be based on fact and reality rather than fancy, illusion, or imagination
options.C: Because metaphysics provides the curriculum content for all subjects
options.D: Because it eliminates the need for religious instruction

questions.explanation: Metaphysics is central to education because it is important that educational programs are grounded in fact and reality rather than illusion or imagination.

questions.question: What is the formal definition of metaphysics implied in the text?

options.A: The study of moral values and ethical behavior
options.B: The study of knowledge and its limits
options.C: The study of ultimate reality
options.D: The study of the structure of arguments

questions.explanation: The text defines metaphysics as 'the study of ultimate reality.'

questions.question: What is the relationship between varying metaphysical beliefs and educational systems?

options.B: Varying metaphysical beliefs lead to differing educational approaches and even separate systems of education
options.C: All metaphysical views converge on the same educational system
options.D: Metaphysical beliefs only affect higher education

questions.explanation: The text explicitly states that varying metaphysical beliefs lead to differing educational approaches and even separate systems of education.

questions.question: Can human activity escape the domain of metaphysics?

options.A: Yes, scientific and practical activities are metaphysics-free
options.B: Yes, but only education can transcend metaphysical assumptions
options.C: No, education cannot escape metaphysics any more than any other human activity
options.D: Only religious activities are tied to metaphysical assumptions

questions.explanation: The text states that 'Education cannot escape the realm of metaphysics any more than any other human activity,' implying no human activity is free of metaphysical assumptions.

questions.question: Why do Christians invest heavily in building their own educational institutions?

options.A: Because public education is of poor academic quality
options.B: Because of their metaphysical beliefs about God, reality, and man's role as God's child
options.C: Because religious law requires separate schooling

questions.explanation: Christians invest millions in education because of their metaphysical beliefs about the nature of ultimate reality, the existence and role of God, and man's nature as God's child.

questions.question: What motivates men and women of the church to be willing to live and die for their educational convictions?

options.B: Political ideology
options.C: Their metaphysical beliefs

questions.explanation: The text states that men and women of the church are motivated by metaphysical beliefs and are willing to live and die for these convictions.

questions.question: What is the ultimate goal Christians seek to achieve through their educational environments?

options.B: Political influence over government
options.C: Creating environments where their basic metaphysical beliefs are taught and practiced by all
options.D: Providing free education for the poor

questions.explanation: Christians desire to create educational environments in which their basic beliefs will be taught and practiced by all.

questions.question: Which of the following best summarizes what metaphysical beliefs determine in an educational context?

options.A: The budget and staffing of schools
options.B: The foundational assumptions about reality upon which educational programs are built
options.C: The extracurricular activities offered
options.D: The physical design of school buildings

questions.explanation: Metaphysical beliefs determine the foundational assumptions about reality — what is real, what is true — on which educational programs are constructed.

questions.question: Which pairing correctly matches a metaphysical question to its domain?

options.A: Does man have a soul? — Economics
options.B: Is man born good or evil? — Human nature / Metaphysics
options.C: What laws should govern society? — Metaphysics
options.D: How should taxes be collected? — Metaphysics

questions.explanation: Whether man is born good, evil, or morally neutral is a metaphysical and philosophical question about human nature.

questions.question: In the sequence of Biblical worldview pillars, which event directly follows the fall of man?

options.B: God's initiative in the incarnation of Jesus Christ
options.C: The inability of man to restore God's image without divine aid
options.D: The calling out of the Church

questions.explanation: After the fall results in partial loss of God's image (pillar e), the next pillar (f) is man's inability — without divine help — to change his nature or restore that image.

questions.question: What distinguishes the Christian metaphysical framework from purely philosophical metaphysics, according to the text?

options.B: Christian metaphysics is grounded in biblical revelation as God's self-disclosure
options.C: Christian metaphysics is identical to secular philosophy
options.D: Christian metaphysics focuses only on ethics

questions.explanation: Christians ground their metaphysical framework in the Bible as the self-revelation of God through Jesus Christ, which provides a basis beyond unaided human reason.

questions.question: Which branch of philosophy is primarily concerned with studying the nature, sources, and validity of truth and knowledge?

options.B: Epistemology
options.C: Ethics

questions.explanation: Epistemology is defined as the branch of philosophy that studies the nature, sources, and validity of truth and knowledge.

questions.question: What is one of the central questions that epistemology seeks to answer?

options.B: What is morally right?
options.C: How do we know?
options.D: What is the purpose of life?

questions.explanation: Epistemology seeks to answer questions such as 'What is true?' and 'How do we know?' — dealing with the dependability and methods of reaching truth.

questions.question: Epistemology stands at the very center of the education process alongside which other branch of philosophy?

options.B: Aesthetics
options.C: Logic

questions.explanation: Epistemology deals with the dependability of knowledge and proper methods of reaching truth, placing it alongside metaphysics at the center of the education process.

questions.question: Why is the question 'Can reality be known?' considered a logical starting point for epistemology?

options.A: It is the simplest possible philosophical question
options.B: It demonstrates the close connection between epistemology and metaphysics
options.C: It was the first question posed by ancient Greek philosophers
options.D: It separates epistemology from all other branches of philosophy

questions.explanation: The question 'Can reality be known?' is a logical starting point for the epistemological venture because it demonstrates the close connection between epistemology and metaphysics.

questions.question: In its narrow sense, skepticism is best described as the position that:

options.A: Knowledge is entirely subjective and varies by individual
options.B: Only scientific knowledge can be considered valid
options.C: It is impossible to gain knowledge and the search for truth is vain
options.D: Truth exists but cannot be communicated effectively

questions.explanation: In its narrow sense, skepticism claims that it is impossible to gain knowledge and that the search for truth is vain.

questions.question: Which ancient Greek philosopher held the skeptical view that nothing exists, and that if it did, we could not know it?

options.B: Plato
options.C: Aristotle

questions.explanation: Gorgias (483–376 BC), a Greek Sophist, asserted that nothing exists and that if it did, we could not know it — a classic expression of narrow skepticism.

questions.question: Gorgias of Leontini, associated with skepticism, lived approximately during which period?
questions.explanation: Gorgias is identified in the text as living from 483 to 376 BC.

questions.question: Gorgias is historically classified as belonging to which group of ancient Greek thinkers?

options.B: Epicureans
options.C: Sophists

questions.explanation: Gorgias is identified as a Greek Sophist who held the skeptical position that nothing exists and that knowledge is unattainable.

questions.question: Agnosticism, as described in the context of epistemology, is best understood as:

options.A: A positive denial of all valid knowledge
options.B: A profession of ignorance, especially regarding the existence or non-existence of God
options.C: The belief that all knowledge is scientifically verifiable
options.D: The view that truth is absolute and unchanging

questions.explanation: Agnosticism is described as a profession of ignorance, especially in reference to the existence or non-existence of God, rather than a positive denial of any valid knowledge.

questions.question: What is the key distinction between agnosticism and skepticism?

options.A: Agnosticism denies all knowledge; skepticism only questions religious knowledge
options.B: Skepticism is concerned only with science; agnosticism applies to all fields
options.C: Agnosticism is a profession of ignorance, not a positive denial of valid knowledge
options.D: Skepticism accepts relative truth; agnosticism does not

questions.explanation: Agnosticism is a profession of ignorance (especially about God's existence), not a positive denial of any valid knowledge — distinguishing it from outright skepticism.

questions.question: Which of the following characteristics does NOT describe relative truth?

options.A: It may be true today and false tomorrow
options.B: It is limited and arbitrary
options.C: It is eternally and universally true

questions.explanation: Being 'eternally and universally true irrespective of time or place' describes Absolute Truth, not relative truth. Relative truth can change, is limited, and may be arbitrary or incomplete.

questions.question: From a Christian philosophical standpoint, Absolute Truth is defined as truth that is:

options.B: Discoverable only through reason
options.C: Eternally and universally true irrespective of time or place

questions.explanation: Absolute Truth in a Christian point of view refers to truth which is eternally and universally true irrespective of time or place.

questions.question: A truth that is considered 'relative' would best be illustrated by which of the following?

options.A: A mathematical theorem proven valid across all number systems
options.B: A social norm that is acceptable in one era but rejected in another
options.C: A physical constant that remains the same throughout the universe
options.D: A divine command believed to apply to all humanity

questions.explanation: Relative truths are those that may be true today but false tomorrow — they are limited, arbitrary, and time/context-dependent, much like shifting social norms.

questions.question: The statement in John 14:6, 'I am the way, the truth, and the life,' is used in the text to illustrate which concept?

options.B: The subjective nature of all truth
options.C: Absolute Truth that cannot be changed

questions.explanation: The text uses John 14:6 to argue that Jesus is the truth and cannot be changed, supporting the idea of an Absolute Truth that is eternal and universal.

questions.question: According to the text's argument about Absolute Truth in education, if such truth exists in the universe, what should be done with it?

options.A: It should be kept within religious institutions only
options.B: It should be discovered and placed at the center of the school curriculum
options.C: It should be debated but never taught as fact
options.D: It should be left to individual students to determine

questions.explanation: The text argues that if Absolute Truth exists in the universe, it would be helpful to discover it and place it at the very center of the school curriculum.

questions.question: The question of whether knowledge is subjective or objective is described as being closely related to which other epistemological issue?

options.B: The relativity of truth
options.C: The limits of scientific method

questions.explanation: The text states that whether knowledge is subjective or objective is closely related to the relativity of truth.

questions.question: Morris (1961) identified how many basic positions on the objectivity of knowledge?

options.B: Four
options.C: Three

questions.explanation: Morris (1961) noted that there are three basic positions on the objectivity of knowledge.

questions.question: Which of the three positions on the objectivity of knowledge holds that knowledge comes from the 'outside' and is inserted into our minds — similar to loading goods onto a ship?

options.B: Knowledge as pure subject manufacture
options.C: Knowledge as objective external input

questions.explanation: The first position holds that knowledge comes from the 'outside' and is inserted into our minds and nervous systems, much like iron ore dumped into a ship — an objective, external-input view.

questions.question: According to Morris (1961), which group of professionals typically views knowledge as something received from the outside, inserted into the mind?

options.B: Social scientists
options.C: Mathematicians and physical scientists

questions.explanation: The text states that mathematicians and physical scientists often see knowledge as something that comes from the outside and is inserted into minds and nervous systems.

questions.question: The second position on the objectivity of knowledge, associated with social scientists, suggests that the knower:

options.A: Receives knowledge passively without contributing to it
options.B: Creates truth independently of the external world
options.C: Contributes to the structure of knowledge through engagement with the world
options.D: Can only know what is divinely revealed

questions.explanation: The second position holds that the knower contributes something to their engagement with the world, being responsible for the structure of their knowledge — a view associated with social scientists.

questions.question: Which group of professionals is specifically associated with the view that the knower actively contributes to the structure of knowledge through their engagement with the world?

options.B: Mathematicians
options.C: Artists

questions.explanation: Social scientists see knowledge in the light of the knower contributing something to the engagement with the world, thereby shaping the structure of knowledge.

questions.question: The third position on the objectivity of knowledge, associated with artists and musicians, holds that humans exist as pure subjects who:

options.A: Receive knowledge from external scientific observation
options.B: Become the manufacturers of truth rather than its recipients or participants
options.C: Passively absorb divine revelation

questions.explanation: The third viewpoint is that we exist as pure subjects who become the manufacturers of truth rather than either its recipients or participants — a view associated with artists and musicians.

questions.question: Which of the following best distinguishes the third position on knowledge objectivity from the first two?

options.A: The third position denies that truth exists at all
options.B: In the third position, humans manufacture truth rather than receive or participate in it
options.C: The third position holds that truth comes entirely from God
options.D: The third position is the only one that acknowledges subjective experience

questions.explanation: Unlike the first position (knowledge as external input) and the second (knowledge as co-constructed), the third position sees humans as pure subjects who manufacture truth themselves.

questions.question: How does epistemology's concern with the 'dependability of knowledge' relate to education?

options.A: It determines how schools are architecturally designed
options.B: It questions which methods of reaching truth are appropriate to teach
options.C: It focuses exclusively on measuring student performance
options.D: It limits education to only empirically verifiable subjects

questions.explanation: Epistemology deals with the dependability of knowledge and the propriety of various methods of reaching truth, making it central to decisions about what and how to teach in education.

questions.question: A truth that answers 'yes' to the questions of being relative, limited, arbitrary, or incomplete would best be classified as:

options.B: Divine Truth
options.C: Relative Truth

questions.explanation: The text states that truths that would answer yes to whether they are relative, limited, arbitrary, powerful, or complete are relative truths.

questions.question: Which branch of philosophy is primarily concerned with the question of whether truth is independent of human experience?

options.B: Epistemology
options.C: Ethics

questions.explanation: The text explicitly states that the question of whether truth is independent of human experience is basic to epistemology.

questions.question: A priori knowledge is best described as knowledge that:

options.A: Depends entirely on sensory experience for validation
options.B: Changes based on cultural and social contexts
options.C: Exists independently of human experience and awareness
options.D: Is derived from careful observation of the physical world

questions.explanation: A priori knowledge is built into the fabric of reality, independent of human knowledge, and true whether or not any human knows or accepts it.

questions.question: Which of the following best illustrates a priori knowledge?

options.A: Knowing that one circle is larger than another after measuring them
options.B: The fixed ratio between a circle's diameter and its circumference
options.C: Observing that two circles lie in the same plane
options.D: Discovering the color of a flower through sight

questions.explanation: The ratio between a circle's diameter and circumference is part of the very nature of circles — it exists prior to and independent of human experience, making it a priori.

questions.question: A posteriori knowledge differs from a priori knowledge in that it:

options.A: Is built into the structure of reality itself
options.B: Exists before and independently of human awareness
options.C: Requires human experience for verification

questions.explanation: A posteriori knowledge is dependent on human experience and awareness — knowing the relationship between two specific circles, for example, requires experiential verification.

questions.question: If a person determines that one circle is larger than another by physically measuring them, this knowledge is classified as:

options.B: Revelatory
options.C: A posteriori

questions.explanation: The relationship between two specific circles (e.g., which is larger, whether they share the same plane) requires human experience for verification, making it a posteriori.

questions.question: Why have traditional philosophies generally regarded a priori knowledge as superior?

options.A: It is easier to test and replicate through experimentation
options.B: It represents a fixed, permanent world unaffected by human knowledge
options.C: It is derived directly from divine revelation
options.D: It relies on the reliability of human sensory organs

questions.explanation: Traditional philosophies upheld a priori knowledge because it is thought to represent the fixed and permanent world that is uncontaminated by human knowledge.

questions.question: Empiricism, as a theory of knowledge, holds that knowledge is primarily obtained through:

options.B: Logical deduction from self-evident truths
options.C: The senses — seeing, hearing, smelling, and tasting

questions.explanation: Empiricism is the view that knowledge is obtained through the senses, whereby people form a picture of the world by seeing, hearing, smelling, and tasting.

questions.question: A person steps outside on a dry day and concludes it is dry season based on warmth, birdsong, and the scent of blossoms. This is an example of:

options.B: Revelatory knowledge
options.C: Empirical knowledge derived through the senses

questions.explanation: The person uses sensory input (sight, sound, smell, feeling) to arrive at a conclusion about the season, which is a classic illustration of empirical knowledge.

questions.question: Sensory knowledge rests on a foundational assumption that:

options.A: All truth must be divinely revealed to be valid
options.B: Human sensory mechanisms are dependable and trustworthy
options.C: Reality only exists when perceived by a conscious mind
options.D: Knowledge gained through the senses is always absolute

questions.explanation: Sensory knowledge is built upon assumptions that must be accepted by faith in the dependability of our sensory mechanism.

questions.question: One key advantage of empirical knowledge over other sources is that:

options.A: It is infallible and cannot be questioned
options.B: It originates from an omniscient source
options.C: Many sensory experiences and experiments can be replicated and publicly examined
options.D: It is independent of all human experience

questions.explanation: The advantage of empirical knowledge is that many sensory experiences and experiments are open to both replication and public examination.

questions.question: Revelation as a source of knowledge is understood to be:

options.A: Knowledge derived from systematic scientific observation
options.B: Communication from God concerning the divine will
options.C: Truth constructed through social consensus

questions.explanation: Revelation is described as God's communication concerning the divine will, held by believers to be a distinct and omniscient source of knowledge.

questions.question: Believers in revelation consider it to have a unique advantage over other sources of knowledge because it:

options.A: Can be replicated and tested in laboratory conditions
options.B: Is derived from rational deduction alone
options.C: Comes from an omniscient source not accessible through other epistemological methods
options.D: Is based on the collective sensory experience of a community

questions.explanation: Believers hold that revelation has the distinct advantage of being an omniscient source of information not obtainable through other epistemological methods.

questions.question: Truth obtained through revelation is characterized as:

options.A: Provisional and subject to revision through experimentation
options.B: Absolute (unconditional) and uncontaminated
options.C: Dependent on the individual's sensory perception
options.D: Valid only within specific cultural frameworks

questions.explanation: The truth gained through revelation is believed to be absolute (unconditional) and uncontaminated — not subject to empirical proof or disproof.

questions.question: Which of the following correctly distinguishes revelatory knowledge from empirical knowledge?

options.A: Revelatory knowledge can be replicated; empirical knowledge cannot
options.B: Empirical knowledge is absolute; revelatory knowledge is conditional
options.C: Revelatory knowledge cannot be proved or disproved empirically; empirical knowledge is open to public examination
options.D: Both sources rely equally on the dependability of the human senses

questions.explanation: Revelation cannot be proved or disproved empirically, whereas empirical knowledge is open to replication and public examination — a fundamental distinction between the two sources.

questions.question: The text implies that philosophical schools differ primarily in how they:

options.A: Define the concept of beauty and aesthetic experience
options.B: Align themselves with viewpoints on the objectivity of truth and knowledge
options.C: Approach questions of political governance and justice
options.D: Interpret the role of mathematics in understanding the universe

questions.explanation: The opening of the text notes that various philosophical schools tend to align themselves with one or another viewpoint on the objectivity of truth and knowledge.

questions.question: Which statement about a priori knowledge is accurate?

options.A: It becomes true only after a human verifies it through experience
options.B: It is true regardless of whether any human knows or accepts it
options.C: It is the same as knowledge derived from the senses
options.D: It changes depending on the cultural context in which it is evaluated

questions.explanation: A priori knowledge is independent of human knowledge and is true whether any human knows and accepts it or not — it exists prior to and independent of human experience.

questions.question: Which of the following scenarios would best represent a posteriori knowledge?

options.A: Recognizing that all triangles have interior angles summing to 180 degrees
options.B: Understanding that every circle has a consistent diameter-to-circumference ratio
options.C: Determining whether two specific circles are in the same or different planes
options.D: Accepting that contradictions cannot simultaneously be true

questions.explanation: Whether two circles share the same plane cannot be known without empirical observation — it requires human experience for verification, making it a posteriori.

questions.question: What does the text suggest about the relationship between two specific circles (e.g., whether one is larger)?

options.A: It is fixed and built into the nature of all circles
options.B: It is a priori because circles are geometric shapes
options.C: It is not given and requires experiential verification
options.D: It can be deduced without any observation

questions.explanation: The relation existing between one specific circle and another is not given — one circle may be larger, they may be in the same or different planes — and knowledge of this requires human experience.

questions.question: Empirical knowledge being 'built into the very nature of human experience' means that:

options.A: It exists before and independently of all sensory input
options.B: It is inseparable from the process of perceiving the world through the senses
options.C: It requires no assumptions about the reliability of human perception
options.D: It is only valid when confirmed through divine sources

questions.explanation: The text states that empirical knowledge is built into the very nature of human experience — it arises from sensory interaction with the world.

questions.question: A researcher conducts an experiment, shares the results publicly, and other scientists repeat it to verify the findings. Which property of empirical knowledge does this best illustrate?

options.B: It is independent of human awareness
options.C: It is open to replication and public examination
options.D: It originates from an omniscient source
